doc.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Humor and feeling in music; great singers and lack of new innovators
summary: He says music needs humor and feeling, recalls Billie Holiday and others, and complains that no new innovators have emerged.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You know I wanted to make just one comment about some of the things that you’ve said and what you’ve been telling us about the blues lyrics is that I sense in your music this marvelous sense of humor. Do you think we could have more of that in music today? I think music needs some of that to come back.

I think it would be nice to have some kind of sense of humor in your music as well as seriousness when it comes to like playing say like “My Funny Valentine” or something like that. You can really make a person feel like this is my valentine. Or if you play like “Lover Man” you want to get that same kind of feeling that Billie Holiday had because it © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

was something very unique and very few people are able to capture that type of feelings anymore. She just had that certain voice. And if you notice, there are certain people that come along, maybe every two decades, and they will have like, well, like Sarah Vaughan, like Billie Holiday, Nat King Cole. They have that certain something in their voices, you know, Ella Fitzgerald, there’s just something — that’s another person that’s alive now, that’s still alive, Gloria Lynne, she’s another that has that certain — you don’t hear much about her. But they have, you know like people can be talking and if you got certain something, they’ll stop talking and listen. Gene Ammons had that, he could do that you know. So there’s just a, I don’t know what it is that’s in the plan but it works out that every — well like when Coleman Hawkins came along, when Lester Young came along, Charlie Parker, John Coltrane. Now I don’t know no one else that’s surfaced yet that’s really an innovator like these people so far. They’re all followers and clones, but nobody at the moment is really doing nothing different. They all follow this pattern. I think that’s the highest form of flattery, you know, when somebody want to do something like you do. But I’m just wondering, because all of the great people are dying. Billy Eckstine, all the really great voices, you know.
